paraphrase: At the end of the Dvāpara age Nārada asks Brahmā how, wandering the earth, he may cross Kali; Brahmā: by merely uttering the name of the Lord, the primal Person Nārāyaṇa, one shakes off Kali.

checks.note: E-text 1 (frame) located in the e-text; the passage matches the paraphrase.

paraphrase: The name is: 'hare rāma hare rāma rāma rāma hare hare, hare kṛṣṇa hare kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa hare hare'.

original.text: hare rāma hare rāma rāma rāma hare hare | hare kṛṣṇa hare kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa hare hare
original.edition: Īśādiviṃśottaraśatopaniṣadaḥ (Nirṇayasāgara collection of 120 Upaniṣads), South Indian recension carrying Upaniṣad Brahmayogin's opening maṅgala verses; e-text github.com/sanskrit/raw_etexts vedaH/misc/upaniShat/mixedPF/108_Upanishads.md
original.licence: text public domain; e-text licence unstated

notes: In this Upaniṣad the 'hare rāma' half comes first; in Gauḍīya use the 'hare kṛṣṇa' half usually comes first.

checks.note: E-text 1 (the sixteen names) located in the e-text; the passage matches the paraphrase. The quoted original matches the e-text (5-gram match 1.00 after folding sandhi).

paraphrase: These sixteen names destroy the evils of Kali; no better means is seen in all the Vedas; they destroy the covering of the jīva of sixteen parts, and then the supreme Brahman shines like the sun's rays when clouds disperse.

paraphrase: Asked the rule, Brahmā says there is no rule: whoever recites it, pure or impure, attains the same world, nearness, form and union; by three and a half crore repetitions one is freed of the gravest sins and even of the sin of abandoning all dharmas.

checks.note: E-text 3 located; the passage matches the paraphrase (it begins: 'iti ṣoḍaśakalāvṛtasya jīva-syāvaraṇavināśanam | tataḥ prakāśate paraṃ brahma meghāpāye raviraśmimaṇḍalī-veti…').

paraphrase: At the end of the Dvāpara age Brahmā tells Nārada that by uttering the names of Nārāyaṇa one crosses over the Kali age: the sixteen names 'hare rāma hare rāma rāma rāma hare hare, hare kṛṣṇa hare kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa hare hare' destroy its evils; no better means is found in all the Vedas, and there are no rules for their utterance.
notes: Whole-text reference (short prose Upaniṣad). In this text the Hare Rāma half precedes the Hare Kṛṣṇa half; Gauḍīya practice usually begins with Hare Kṛṣṇa.
